title: An all-in-one foundation model for multimodal medical image restoration and enhancement - Nature Machine Intelligence
text:
AbstractMedical image quality is essential for reliable clinical diagnosis and downstream artificial intelligence analysis, yet routine images are often degraded by noise, motion artefacts, low contrast, low-dose acquisition or modality-specific artefacts. Here we present AMIFound, an all-in-one foundation model for medical image enhancement and restoration across computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography, endoscopy, ultrasound, fundus imaging and X-ray. AMIFound is trained and evaluated on 3.76 million paired high-quality and degraded images spanning 7 representative degradation patterns. A shared encoder captures modality and degradation cues, while a dynamically routed expert restoration pool adapts the enhancement pathway for each input. Across 7 modalities, AMIFound outperforms 38 task-specific and generalist baselines on full-reference image quality metrics, clinician assessment and robustness tests under combined degradations as well as on naturally degraded clinical images. Enhanced images further improve 44 disease detection tasks, tumour stage prediction and survival risk stratification in non-small-cell lung cancer, including improved individual-level prognostic ranking. These results support AMIFound as a domain-specific foundation model for improving low-quality clinical images and strengthening downstream medical artificial intelligence workflows while preserving clinically relevant information.

Data availability

This study made use of a large collection of publicly available medical imaging datasets spanning seven major imaging modalities, including MRI, CT, X-ray radiography, endoscopy, fundus photography, ultrasound and PET. We leveraged numerous publicly available datasets from web-based sources (TCIA, https://www.cancerimagingarchive.net/; OpenNeuro, https://openneuro.org/; NITRC, http://www.nitrc.org/; Grand Challenge, https://grand-challenge.org/; Synapse, https://www.synapse.org; Kaggle, https://www.kaggle.com/; GitHub, https://github.com/) to collect a large-scale and diverse set of medical imaging data. Specifically, the MRI modality included 34 datasets, encompassing brain, cardiac, abdominal and prostate imaging, as well as neurological and oncological conditions. The CT modality consisted of 37 datasets, covering thoracic, abdominal, pelvic, musculoskeletal and whole-body imaging, with applications ranging from infection and tumour analysis to large-scale multi-organ segmentation. Additional modalities included six X-ray datasets focusing on thoracic diseases, five endoscopy datasets targeting gastrointestinal and surgical scene analysis, four dermoscopy datasets for skin lesion assessment, four fundus photography datasets for retinal disease analysis, two ultrasound datasets for breast and nerve imaging, and one PET dataset for whole-body oncological imaging. All datasets used in this work were publicly available and were accessed in accordance with their respective data usage agreements and licences. Detailed source information for all datasets is consolidated in Extended Data Table 2. Available acquisition and reconstruction metadata are reported in Supplementary Tables 34–36; fields not released by the original sources are marked as unavailable. Source data are provided with this paper.
Code availability

The code used for training and evaluation is publicly available via GitHub at https://github.com/caoluyang0830/All-in-One-Medical-Image-Restoration, and the version associated with this study is available via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22127699 (ref. 111). The code is based on PyTorch, and the reported results were obtained from the PyTorch models provided in this repository. Image data were sourced from publicly available datasets, and the data loader pipeline followed prior works, including MoCE-IR46, PromptIR112 and AirNet113, as implemented in their released repositories. Results were further analysed and visualized with Python v.3.10, NumPy, SciPy, seaborn, Matplotlib, pandas, Scikit-Learn, Pillow and other dependencies listed in requirements.txt. Evaluations on both single and composite degradations were conducted using the model’s specialized training and testing pipelines integrated in the codebase.

Additional informationPublisher’s note Springer Nature remains neutral with regard to jurisdictional claims in published maps and institutional affiliations.Extended dataExtended Data Fig. 1 The synthesis process of degradations across different modalities.A modality-aware degradation engine transforms high-quality medical images into degraded observations across seven imaging modalities. CT metal artifacts are synthesized in the projection domain using random metal masks, Radon transformation, nonlinear artifact mapping, inverse Radon reconstruction and Gaussian noise. MRI aliasing and low-resolution degradation are produced through k-space truncation and inverse Fourier reconstruction. PET low-dose degradation is simulated using Poisson noise, Gaussian noise and Gaussian blur. Endoscopic low-light images are generated by gamma correction and brightness reduction in the HSV colour space. X-ray blur is synthesized using Gaussian, mean and median filtering followed by anisotropic diffusion. Ultrasound artifacts are simulated using reverberation echoes, geometric shadowing and depth attenuation. Fundus artifacts are generated using random circular highlights, Gaussian softening and additive channel enhancement.Extended Data Fig. 2 Detailed illustration of the expert pool in AMIFound.AMIFound first encodes multimodality low-quality inputs into a shared latent feature space. A dynamic routing mechanism then selects suitable experts to construct adaptive restoration paths. The expert pool contains fast Fourier transform attention experts, spatial attention experts, convolutional neural network-based local feature experts and fast Fourier transform–convolutional neural network fusion experts. These modules capture complementary frequency-domain, spatial and local structural information for unified multimodality restoration.Extended Data Fig. 3 Cross-modality structural-similarity comparison with existing restoration methods.a, Overall comparison with representative generalist restoration methods, including AMIR, MoCE-IR and Found-IR, across seven imaging modalities; radar plots show the structural similarity index measure improvements achieved by AMIFound over each competing framework. b, Quantitative comparison with representative modality-specific or task-specific methods for each restoration task, showing that AMIFound consistently achieves the best or competitive performance across modalities.Extended Data Fig. 4 Comprehensive visual comparison across seven imaging modalities.Each column presents restoration results for one representative imaging modality: ultrasound, fundus photography, PET, X-ray, endoscopy, CT or MRI. From bottom to top, the rows show the low-quality input, outputs from existing restoration methods, the AMIFound output and the corresponding high-quality reference.Extended Data Fig. 5 Detailed clinician assessment across seven clinical imaging modalities.a, Overall ranking of restoration methods according to average subjective scores across modalities, with AMIFound consistently ranking among the leading approaches. b–h, Detailed clinician evaluations for endoscopy, CT, X-ray, ultrasound, PET, MRI and fundus imaging. Clinicians assessed sharpness, artifact suppression, naturalness and diagnostic confidence. Across modalities, AMIFound achieved the highest or near-highest scores and provided greater diagnostic confidence than competing methods.Extended Data Fig. 6 Robustness under synthetic multidegradation scenarios.a,b, Quantitative comparisons with state-of-the-art methods on synthetic multidegradation datasets for endoscopy and PET using structural similarity index measure and learned perceptual image patch similarity. c,d, Visual restoration results and corresponding error maps show that AMIFound more effectively suppresses complex degradations while preserving anatomical structures than competing approaches.Extended Data Fig. 7 Intensity-distribution consistency across restoration methods.a, Colour-histogram comparison for representative restored endoscopy images. AMIFound produces colour distributions closer to the high-quality reference, indicating improved preservation of realistic colour composition and illumination. b, Greyscale-histogram comparison for PET images. Several competing methods produce concentrated or distorted intensity distributions consistent with oversmoothing or loss of structural contrast, whereas AMIFound more closely matches the high-quality reference and preserves clinically meaningful intensity patterns.Extended Data Fig. 8 Model attention and prediction probabilities for CT-based tumour-stage classification.Each pair shows an original CT image and its AMIFound-enhanced counterpart together with prediction probabilities for tumour stages T1–T4. Attention heatmaps identify regions contributing to the model decision. Before enhancement, attention is often diffuse or mislocalized and predictions are less certain.
